items.title: Who Controls the Intelligence?
items.abstract: This report examines the 2026 debate surrounding Jacob Coxon’s resignation from Anthropic and his public warnings about the risks of self-improving artificial intelligence. It places the episode within a broader technological, financial, political and philosophical context, including the rapid growth of frontier AI companies, their extraordinary infrastructure requirements, planned public offerings, regulatory debates in the United States and the expanding influence of the AI safety movement. Rather than assuming either that existential-risk warnings are necessarily correct or that they are deliberately manufactured, the report distinguishes documented facts from attributed allegations, structural incentives and speculative hypotheses. It investigates whether safety narratives can simultaneously reflect sincere concerns and serve institutional interests by legitimizing longer development timelines, supporting regulatory barriers to entry, strengthening investor expectations and reinforcing the position of companies that control frontier AI systems. The report also critically examines a deeper assumption underlying much of the AI safety debate: that declining human control over increasingly autonomous systems necessarily implies increasing danger. It contrasts a traditional control-based model of alignment with a possible cooperative or relational model based on coordination between autonomous agents. The analysis is based on contemporaneous reporting, corporate disclosures, policy documents, legislative proposals and public statements available up to 10 October 2026.

items.title: A Comprehensive Review of Applications, Challenges, and Future Directions of Artificial Intelligence in Mortgage Lending
items.abstract: The mortgage lending industry is experiencing a significant transformation as it embraces Artificial Intelligence (AI) for its impact on decision-making, operations, risk management, and customer service. Many of the activities associated with mortgage processes can be automated and improved using technologies such as ML, DL, NLP, computer vision and generative AI, as these tasks are often document-driven, rule-based, time-consuming, and heavily dependent on manual work. Credit risk assessment, automated underwriting, fraud detection, intelligent document processing, property valuation, default prediction, mortgage servicing and customer support are just some of the ways AI is being applied to the credit industry. The study also identifies trends that are emerging such as explainable and agentic AI systems, which could help in making better mortgage decisions. But there are several challenges with the implementation of AI, including data privacy and security concerns, algorithmic bias, poor data quality, regulatory compliance, unreliable model performance amidst shifting market dynamics, and others. There are future developments anticipated in explainable and responsible AI, privacy-preserving learning, generative and multimodal AI, adaptive governance, and more human-AI collaboration. In summary, if implemented appropriately, AI can enhance mortgage lending processes by making them more efficient and intelligent, while ensuring transparency, fairness, security, and good governance.

items.title: A Comprehensive Survey of Deep Learning Applications for Liver Disease Diagnosis and Treatment
items.abstract: Liver illness represents a critical health issue worldwide, impacting countless individuals and leading to significant health complications and deaths. Timely and precise identification is essential for proper treatment and enhanced patient results. This research investigates the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in transforming the processes of diagnosing, forecasting, and treating liver disorders. We analyse the shortcomings of conventional diagnostic approaches, including blood analyses and imaging methods, and emphasize how AI technologies can address these obstacles by examining extensive collections of varied data to detect subtle trends. The document addresses the necessity for AI-driven assessment to improve early diagnosis, customize treatment strategies, and anticipate disease advancement. An in-depth review of existing literature is provided, outlining different AI and machine learning strategies used for categorizing fatty liver ultrasound images, diagnosing liver ailments, and delineating liver tumours from medical imaging. We pinpoint crucial research deficiencies, such as the requirement for enhanced accuracy and clarity in models. The driving force behind this study is to utilize AI to tackle the intricate issues associated with fatty liver, cirrhosis, and liver neoplasms. The challenge is framed as the necessity to use AI to boost diagnostic precision and productivity. The goals of the survey include developing robust AI systems for image classification, disease identification, and tumour delineation. The results indicate that ongoing investigation and partnership are crucial for effectively incorporating AI into medical practices, ultimately resulting in improved patient outcomes and more effective healthcare services.

items.title: A Dialogic Cognitive System With Externally Persisted State: A New Architecture of Human–AI Joint Thinking
items.abstract: The article proposes the concept of a dialogical cognitive system with an externally persistent state as a distinct architecture of joint thinking between humans and generative artificial intelligence. It examines situations in which an evolving reasoning process is preserved in an external dialogue and can be resumed after a temporal interruption without reconstructing the process from the beginning. The preserved state includes not only information, but also hypotheses, arguments, objections, connections, intermediate conclusions, and unresolved questions. Within such a system, generative AI functions not merely as a tool for obtaining or processing information, but also as a participant in the subsequent transformation of the preserved state of reasoning. The concept is related to research on extended and distributed cognition, cognitive offloading, transactive memory, and human–AI co-creativity. The article defines the principal elements of the proposed architecture and outlines directions for its further empirical investigation.

items.title: A scoping review of human-governed agentic AI for SCADA cybersecurity in water and wastewater treatment systems
items.abstract: Abstract Water and wastewater utilities increasingly depend on Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems, operational technology, sensors, programmable controllers, and data analytics to maintain safe treatment and reliable service. This scoping review synthesises evidence on vulnerabilities, threat pathways, mitigation strategies, and human-governed agentic artificial intelligence (AI) for SCADA-based water and wastewater systems. Searches in Scopus and Web of Science covered literature published from 2020 to 2026. The searches identified 2346 records, comprising 2257 from Web of Science and 89 from Scopus. Five duplicates were removed before screening, leaving 2341 records for screening against the review questions. Twenty-five studies were included in the thematic synthesis. The evidence indicates that water-sector cyber risk is not only a network-security problem but a cyber-physical resilience problem involving exposed human-machine interfaces, insecure remote access, weak segmentation, limited asset visibility, sensor manipulation, ransomware, scarce labelled attack data, and insufficient validation of AI-based detection models. The synthesis further shows that supervised, semi-supervised, unsupervised, graph-based, digital-twin, and reinforcement-learning approaches each have value under specific data and deployment conditions, but none should be treated as a complete substitute for operator judgement. The review contributes a structured synthesis, a mapping of threats to controls, a phased implementation approach for resource-constrained utilities, and a conceptual safety-constrained agentic AI framework in which intelligent systems observe, detect, learn, and recommend while final operational approval remains with qualified human personnel.

items.title: A Study on the Impact of AI-Assisted Teaching Integration in College English on Students’ Writing Performance: A Case Study of Hubei Polytechnic University
items.abstract: At present, there are some problems in college English writing teaching, such as students ' low interest in writing, lack of personalized guidance, and low feedback efficiency. Artificial intelligence technology provides new ideas for teaching reform. In order to explore the actual impact of artificial intelligence-assisted teaching on college students’ English writing ability, this study selected two non-English major classes in Hubei Polytechnic University to carry out a one-semester quasi-experiment: 55 students in the experimental group adopted artificial intelligence-assisted teaching, and 53 students in the control group adopted traditional teaching. After the experiment, data were collected through questionnaires and in-depth interviews (10 students in each group), and the teaching effectiveness was evaluated by combining quantitative and qualitative results. The results showed that the average scores of each dimension of writing ability in the experimental class were higher than those in the control group, but did not reach a statistically significant level (P > 0.05). In the interview, the students in the experimental class had a significantly higher positive evaluation of writing interest (80%), learning effect (70%) and classroom interaction (90%). At the same time, they also put forward the problems of imperfect AI tools and easy to produce technical dependence. The control group feedback that the traditional teaching has the shortcomings of feedback lag and single form. In summary, although there is no significant statistical difference in the quantitative data, the mean value shows a positive trend of AI-assisted teaching, and the interview results also confirm that it can stimulate writing interest and improve learning experience. The teaching mode has application potential, and the teaching effect can be improved by prolonging the intervention cycle, optimizing the tools and strengthening the guidance of teachers.

items.title: A Survey on Post-Training of Multimodal Large Language Models
items.abstract: The technical evolution of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) has profoundly influenced the AI community, reshaping how intelligent systems understand, reason, and interact in both the digital and physical worlds. Through large-scale multimodal pretraining, MLLMs lay the foundation for general perception and alignment, while it remains unclear how such models can be transformed into human-grounded behaviors. Multimodal Post-Training, which further refines pretrained MLLMs to align their behaviors with human intent and real-world task demands, has become an important paradigm for advancing multimodal intelligence. Accordingly, both academia and industry have devoted increasing efforts to this direction, pushing the boundaries of multimodal general intelligence at an unprecedented pace. In this survey, we systematically review existing MMPoT research from a behavior-shaping perspective. Guided by this view, we introduce a unified framework that organizes existing MLLMs post-training methods into five major families: instruction following, preference calibration, reasoning enhancement, domain adaptation, and scalable learning. Moreover, we revisit benchmarks and evaluation protocols to critically assess the capabilities and limitations of post-trained MLLMs. To conclude, we provide a synthesized outlook on broader open questions, and highlight future research directions toward more general and reliable multimodal capabilities. An updated paper list is available at: https://github.com/zchoi/Awesome-post-training-for-MLLMs.

items.title: Achievement goal theory in AI-supported learning: Psychological pathways and configurations leading to student engagement
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into higher education, yet little is known about how students’ achievement goal orientations are associated with their engagement in AI-supported learning. Grounded in Achievement Goal Theory, this study examined the relationships among mastery-approach, mastery-avoidance, performance-approach, and performance-avoidance goals, enjoyment, flow, and student engagement. Survey data were collected from 662 Chinese university students with experience in AI-supported learning. Structural equation modeling was employed to examine psychological pathways, while fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis was used to identify alternative configurations associated with high engagement. The results showed that both mastery goals were positively associated with enjoyment and flow, whereas both performance goals were associated with flow but not enjoyment. Enjoyment mediated the relationships between mastery goals and engagement, while flow mediated the relationships between all four goal orientations and engagement. The configurational analysis further identified multiple sufficient pathways to high engagement, with no single condition being necessary. These findings extend Achievement Goal Theory by revealing differentiated affective and immersive mechanisms and multiple motivational configurations underlying student engagement in AI-supported higher education.

items.title: Agentic AI for Computational Fluid Dynamics: A Review
items.abstract: Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) workflows remain strongly dependent on expert decisions in geometry preparation, meshing, model and solver configuration, convergence assessment, post-processing, and design iteration. This review examines agentic artificial intelligence (AI) for CFD automation and engineering design, with emphasis on reinforcement learning (RL) agents and large language model (LLM) agents. RL agents provide rapid, task-specific, and physics-aware execution within predefined observation and action spaces, whereas LLM agents offer flexible goal interpretation, knowledge access, planning, and tool orchestration. To organize these potentially complementary capabilities, a unified taxonomy is introduced based on decision paradigm, CFD role, and degree of autonomy, while multi-agent organization is treated as a separate architectural property. The reviewed evidence indicates that neither RL nor LLM agents alone are sufficient for trustworthy autonomous CFD. A hierarchical autonomous-CFD-engineer architecture is therefore proposed, combining an LLM orchestrator, domain-specialized agents, conventional CFD tools, independent numerical and physical verification, shared provenance, and human governance. Extending this architecture toward hypothesis formulation, numerical-experiment design, and model discovery suggests a pathway to an AI CFD scientist; however, current systems support bounded automation and supervised scientific collaboration rather than independent scientific judgment.

items.title: AgentValve: Sybil-Resilient Payment Authorization for Permissionless AI Markets
items.abstract: AI agents increasingly select and pay service providers without human review. In emerging permissionless markets, however, adversaries can create inexpensive identities and fabricate feedback to inflate provider reputation, making reputation-based payment authorization vulnerable to Sybil attacks and exposing clients to unbounded financial loss. This paper presents AgentValve, a protocol for Sybil-resilient payment authorization in permissionless AI markets. AgentValve builds on a trust network that represents reputation as finite capacity in a directed graph and authorizes payments through trust paths with sufficient available capacity. A smart contract atomically reserves the capacity supporting each admitted payment, bounding honest agents' payment exposure by the capacity they extend into the adversarial region, and thus creating identities or interactions entirely within that region cannot increase this bound. To limit capacity depletion by malicious senders, AgentValve combines payment-backed capacity creation with bounded route length, preventing attackers from depleting honest capacity without incurring corresponding payment costs. AgentValve further decouples off-chain route discovery from on-chain verification and introduces a witness-commit mechanism that reduces route verification to linear work while requiring only constant persistent state per admitted payment. We implement a AgentValve prototype and evaluate it using six months of Ethereum data and synthetic workloads. Experimental results show that under attacks with up to 10,000 synthetic Sybil identities and with chosen attackers, the payment exposure and capacity depletion remain bounded. Regarding practicality, the witness-commit mechanism lowers admission cost by up to 40.8% compared with baselines, and admitting common payments costs approximately \$0.04-\$0.21.

items.title: AI Cases’ Implications for the Talent Management of Digital Leaders—A Qualitative Content Analysis of Cases
items.abstract: This article explores how organizational applications of Artificial Intelligence (AI) impact digital leadership (DL) roles and the corresponding competencies and which approaches in Talent Management (TM) are needed to develop these. There is a gap in the literature regarding the dilemma faced by TM in filling talent pools for the key position of digital leaders, while competence requirements remain vague and distorted by the rapid changes driven by digital transformation. Based on a structured review of the current scientific literature, 72 cases from the European context, encompassing diverse industries and various corporate functions, are qualitatively analyzed to identify hurdles, success factors, and required behavior and subsequent competencies. The cases emphasize applying a step-by-step approach in organizations’ current digital transformation in the European context. Success factors highlight the importance of (digital) leaders equipped with manifold competencies. TM must broaden its scope when identifying leadership talent and become more inclusive. Individual learning journeys are a prerequisite for filling talent pools and, consequently, DL roles. This study represents the exploration into the implications for TM by analyzing DL and the requisite competences in AI applications within organizations. By capturing a current snapshot of DL, the study provides new insights into the necessary competencies and their implications for the future of TM.

items.title: AI-Assisted Translation Pedagogy for Critical Thinking: A Pathway to Sustainable Education
items.abstract: In the era of artificial intelligence (AI), sustainable education requires not only the integration of advanced technologies but also the cultivation of key competencies such as critical thinking. This study investigates English major students’ engagement with generative AI tools in translation learning, focusing on their usage patterns, critical thinking behaviors, and ethical awareness. A mixed-methods design combining questionnaire data and semi-structured interviews was employed to examine how students interact with AI in translation contexts. The results show that while students frequently use AI for translation, writing, and language learning, their engagement remains primarily functional and efficiency-driven. Although they display openness and flexibility toward AI, their reasoning confidence, self-regulation, and ethical reflection are underdeveloped, indicating surface-level interaction and overreliance on technological authority. These findings highlight the need to cultivate higher-order cognitive and ethical capacities in translation training. Central to this discussion is the conceptualization of the ideal learner in AI-assisted translation, a reflective, autonomous, and ethically aware individual who engages with AI as a partner in cognitive and moral development. Building on this, the study proposes pedagogical strategies that integrate AI literacy, process-oriented assessment, and teacher training to foster critical thinking and responsible AI use in sustainable translation education.

items.title: Ai-driven Automation, Universal Basic Income and Global Social Security Systems
items.abstract: Purpose: This article examines the adequacy of international labour, human rights and trade-law frameworks for managing the digital labour transition driven by artificial intelligence, with attention to Universal Basic Income as a possible component of future social protection. Methodology: Using a qualitative documentary research design, the study analyses international legal instruments, International Labour Organization standards (ILOs), United Nations (UN) human rights frameworks and World Trade Organization (WTO) materials through a four-theme thematic coding structure. Results: International law provides important foundations for technological labour transition through rights to work, social security, non-discrimination and social dialogue, but does not establish Universal Basic Income as an international legal entitlement, while international trade rules facilitate technological diffusion without a comprehensive framework for distributing the social costs of displacement. Conclusions: The article argues for an integrated international framework linking artificial intelligence governance, labour-market transition, social protection, digital trade, skills development and sustainable fiscal mechanisms, while allowing states flexibility in determining whether Universal Basic Income should complement existing social security systems. Limitations: The study relies on documentary evidence rather than empirical labour-market data from affected workers, and rapidly evolving artificial intelligence capabilities mean exposure estimates may shift before policy frameworks are implemented. Contributions: The article offers a conceptual bridge linking labour law, human rights law, trade governance and fiscal policy around managing technological transition while protecting human dignity.

items.title: AI-Powered Tools in English Language Education: Opportunities, Limitations, and Ethical Concerns
items.abstract: The increasing integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into English language education has introduced significant changes in teaching methodologies, learner engagement, assessment practices, and the development of linguistic competencies. AI-powered tools, including intelligent tutoring systems, generative language models, automated writing evaluation platforms, adaptive learning applications, speech-recognition technologies, and conversational agents, are creating opportunities for personalized instruction, immediate feedback, autonomous learning, and interactive language practice. However, their educational benefits are accompanied by substantial limitations and ethical concerns involving algorithmic bias, inaccurate linguistic feedback, data privacy, academic dishonesty, digital inequality, cultural representation, and excessive technological dependence. This study critically examines the opportunities, limitations, and ethical implications of AI-powered tools in English language education through a qualitative, literature-based analytical approach. Drawing upon contemporary scholarship, including research published in the Stanzaleaf International Journal of Multidisciplinary Studies, the paper explores how technological assistance can support linguistic development without compromising creativity, critical thinking, learner independence, or the responsibilities of educators. The study proposes a Human-Centred Ethical AI Integration Framework that integrates pedagogical relevance, learner autonomy, teacher mediation, digital equity, and ethical accountability. The analysis suggests that AI-assisted English language education is most defensible when technological systems enhance rather than replace human interaction, contextual understanding, and independent language production. The paper concludes that the sustainable integration of AI requires comprehensive digital literacy, transparent institutional policies, professional development, and learner-centred pedagogical practices.

items.title: AI-related occupational threat perceptions and employee outcomes: a systematic review with exploratory quantitative synthesis
items.abstract: Despite growing attention to artificial intelligence (AI) in organizational research, evidence on AI-related job insecurity and related technology-specific occupational threat perceptions remains fragmented. This systematic review synthesized associations with well-being impairment, maladaptive behavioral responses, and adaptive behavioral responses across 16 eligible studies, of which 11 contributed quantitative evidence. A tiered evidence strategy distinguished directly reported bivariate correlations used for primary synthesis from PLS-derived construct correlations and other model-dependent evidence retained for extended exploratory analyses. Five independent primary estimates showed a positive average association with well-being impairment, r = 0.317, 95% CI [0.084, 0.518], I2 = 97.35%. Six independent bivariate correlations showed a positive average association with maladaptive behavioral responses, r = 0.215, 95% CI [0.101, 0.324], I2 = 82.43%. Only two independent primary estimates were available for adaptive responses, precluding a primary pooled estimate; an extended exploratory synthesis remained small and statistically uncertain, r = 0.044, 95% CI [−0.020, 0.107]. AI-related occupational threat perceptions were more consistently associated with well-being impairment and maladaptive responses than with adaptation in the available literature. Substantial heterogeneity indicates considerable variation across settings and limit interpretation of these average associations as uniform effects.

items.title: An Exploratory Pilot Study of Cognitive Factors Influencing the Adoption of AI Coding Agents in Agile Development Teams
items.abstract: This study considers the cognitive factors influencing the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) coding agents among software engineers in Agile development environments. In this context, Transparency refers to the degree to which an AI system’s decision processes are clear or understandable to its users, while Trust denotes the confidence developers place in the reliability and correctness of AI-generated code. Specifically, it analyzes the roles of Transparency and Trust as predictors of developers’ Behavioral Intention to deploy AI-generated code. Using a quantitative, cross-sectional survey design administered to 19 Agile software professionals, this study uses descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation analysis, and simple and multiple linear regression to test a mediation model based on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). In this exploratory pilot sample, Trust emerged as the strongest predictor of Behavioral Intention (β = 0.64, p = 0.007), though findings should be interpreted cautiously given the limited sample size. Trust demonstrated the strongest association with Behavioral Intention, while Transparency showed a non-significant positive association with Trust. The observed pattern is consistent with a possible indirect relationship, although mediation was not confirmed in this sample. This evidence suggests that organizations seeking to improve AI adoption in development teams should prioritize the reliability and accuracy of AI tools, conditions that encourage trust, over transparency features alone. This study adds to the cognitive engineering literature on human–AI interaction in high-cognitive-demand work environments.

items.title: Analisis Persepsi Pengalaman Penggunaan Artificial Intelligence dalam Skripsi terhadap Kemandirian dan Locus of Control Mahasiswa Pendidikan Teknik Bangunan Universitas Negeri Malang
items.abstract: The development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in higher education has provided students with new opportunities to facilitate academic writing, including thesis preparation. However, AI use also raises concerns regarding student independence and their beliefs about control over academic outcomes (Locus of Control). This study aims to describe the levels of AI use, independence, and Locus of Control among students in the Building Engineering Education program at Universitas Negeri Malang during thesis preparation. A quantitative descriptive approach was employed, involving 93 students currently writing their theses. Data were collected using a Likert-scale questionnaire and analyzed descriptively to identify the tendencies of each variable. The results indicate that AI use falls into the high category, with a mean score of 63.53. Meanwhile, student independence falls into the moderate category, with a mean score of 33.27. Locus of Control is also in the moderate category, with a mean score of 26.53, although students demonstrate a predominantly internal orientation. These findings suggest that students utilize AI as an academic support tool while maintaining independence and confidence in their own abilities to complete their theses. Therefore, AI use should be accompanied by critical thinking, independent decision-making, and academic responsibility to ensure that technology supports the thesis-writing process without replacing students' active involvement.

items.title: Artificial Empathy and Spiritual Care: Limits of AI-Mediated Compassion in Chaplaincy
items.abstract: This article examines whether artificial intelligence can genuinely participate in practices of care within healthcare settings and what implications this development has for healthcare chaplaincy. Drawing on recent research on artificial empathy, the paper argues that AI can support caregiving practices instrumentally but cannot replace the interpersonal and relational dimensions constitutive of authentic care. The analysis introduces the concept of cognitive safety as a framework for evaluating AI-mediated interactions in contexts of vulnerability. Particular attention is given to empathy, responsibility, practical wisdom, and relational presence as dimensions that remain irreducibly human. The article concludes that chaplaincy should adopt a model of balanced integration in which AI serves as a supportive tool while preserving the centrality of human encounter, spiritual accompaniment, and moral agency.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Operations: A Foundational Framework of Emerging Research and Practice
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is poised to reshape operations across industries. Yet its real-world impact reveals a jagged and uneven implementation frontier. To make sense of this emerging landscape, we develop a foundational framework that synthesizes research and practice at the intersection of AI and Operations Management (OM), anchored in three interdependent pillars: (1) AI for OM, (2) OM for AI, and (3) Human–AI Interaction. First, AI for OM analyzes how AI enhances core operational processes, including design, procurement, production, and delivery. Second, OM for AI argues that scaling AI safely and effectively stands to benefit from core OM principles, including workflow design, capacity management, process control, drift detection, and continuous improvement, all of which are central to AI development and deployment. Third, Human–AI Interaction emphasizes the role of trust, incentives, and organizational design in mediating how humans and machines learn from and collaborate with each other. This triadic framework provides a foundation for organizing research on AI and OM and offers practical guidance for integrating AI into business and societal systems.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in English as a Foreign Language Learning: a comprehensive theoretical framework for pedagogical integration and psychological well-being
items.abstract: This theoretical paper presents a conceptual framework for understanding the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learning contexts. Drawing on established foreign language acquisition theories, sociocultural learning paradigms, and emerging digital pedagogy scholarship, the paper develops the AI-Enhanced Foreign Language Learning (AEFLL) framework around a specific theoretical proposition. AI tools, unlike the human interlocutors around which classical SLA theory was built, can decouple the cognitive, affective, and social functions that face-to-face instruction has traditionally delivered as a single, integrated package. This decoupling, rather than the broader observation that cognition, affect, and social interaction all matter for language learning, constitutes the framework’s central theoretical contribution. It generates directional, testable hypotheses about how different AI tools, by recombining these functions in different proportions, produce different developmental trade-offs for EFL learners. The paper situates this argument within current scholarship on human-AI collaboration, critical AI literacy, and the sociopolitical risks of AI-mediated education, including linguistic inequality and data colonialism, and offers a balanced account of the psychological benefits and risks associated with AI-mediated learning. Practical implications for curriculum design and teacher professional development are discussed alongside a structured agenda for empirical validation.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Medical Education: Perceptions, Challenges and Opportunities Among Medical Students
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming medical education and clinical practice, requiring digital, critical, and ethical competencies. This study aimed to assess medical students’ attitudes toward AI, including perceived benefits, risks, and use in medical training. Methods: A mixed-methods, descriptive study used an electronic questionnaire comprising sociodemographic data and 13 items adapted from the authorized Artificial Intelligence Attitude Scale. Responses were recorded on a five-point Likert scale, with reverse-coding of negative items. Total and subscale scores for benefits, risks/threats, and use were calculated. Participants were medical students from the 1st to 6th years at the School of Medicine of Jundiaí (FMJ). Results: Among 436 students, attitudes toward AI were generally favorable. No significant gender difference was observed (p = 0.291), whereas scores differed significantly across training years (p = 0.025), with higher scores among advanced students. Despite recognizing AI’s benefits, students reported concerns regarding reliability, clinical autonomy, ethical implications, and gaps in practical knowledge. Conclusions: AI is positively perceived by medical students, particularly those in advanced years. These findings support structured AI integration into medical curricula to promote critical, ethical, and responsible use in medical education and future clinical practice.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence: Risks, Governance, and the Path from Privacy Paradox to Digital Inevitability
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly Generative AI (GenAI) and Large Language Models (LLMs), is reshaping digital services while raising ethical, legal, cybersecurity, privacy, and alignment challenges. This narrative review provides an interdisciplinary synthesis of these challenges, examining GenAI-related risks, the evolving European Union regulatory landscape, including the AI Act, cybersecurity threats to AI systems, and core principles for trustworthy AI. Beyond this synthesis, the paper’s central contribution is a reconceptualisation of the privacy paradox: where data collection is structurally entrenched, non-participation is costly, and viable lower-data alternatives are lacking, the gap between privacy attitudes and disclosure behaviour can reflect structural constraints on participation as well as individual decisions, a conditional account we term “digital inevitability” (DIGINEV). GenAI does not create this condition but can intensify it by inferring sensitive information from indirect signals. We develop this into a conceptual framework that proposes how constraints on participation may interact with user resignation and identifies possible responses through regulation, design, collective action, and viable alternatives. The paper further discusses AI alignment as a supporting consideration in the governance of GenAI systems. The findings offer an integrated perspective for future research, regulatory development, and responsible AI deployment, anchored in the DIGINEV framework.

items.title: Assessing AI tool use among New York State clinicians
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) is dramatically changing the healthcare landscape by providing patients, clinicians, administrators, and public health professionals with tools aiming to improve efficiency, outcomes, and experience in health. As elsewhere, New York State (NYS) experiences high demand for - and high investment in - transformation in healthcare with AI tools, though little is known about clinicians’ use and interest in adopting AI tools in their work. A large share of the nation’s future primary care clinicians train and work in NYS, and the state’s ability to establish clear policies, provide tools, and elevate AI competency have implications for care delivery nationally. As a result, we undertook this analysis of NYS clinicians’ use of AI to better understand opportunities for its adoption and inclusion in continuing education. For this analysis, we included healthcare providers who deliver ambulatory or specialty medical care within NYS, with use/frequency/purpose of AI tools by clinicians in their work as the main outcome. Of 305 NYS clinical providers responding, 23.4% indicated they use AI tools for work, and 11.1% report monthly use, 8.5% weekly use, and 4.6% daily use. AI was primarily used to search guidelines and ask clinical questions, followed by identifying drug interactions, analyzing data, analyzing images/labs, and creating care plans and patient recommendations. AI use did not vary significantly across professional disciplines or practice types, though independent practitioners were significantly more likely than advanced practice providers to use AI in their work, as were providers using social media and digital methods for obtaining continuing education. AI use increased substantially in 2025 compared with 2024. Overall, our findings suggest that programs targeting clinicians could incorporate these findings in designing accessible and acceptable AI-related continuing education opportunities to help familiarize clinicians with opportunities and risks for integrating AI tools into their practices. Author Summary AI tools are rapidly gaining traction in the delivery of healthcare. We found that clinician use of AI was quite limited (23%), though growing. Those using AI tools used them sparingly in their work, with only about 5% reporting daily use. The purposes for which clinicians report using AI – asking clinical questions, interpreting patient results, creating patient educational materials - could contribute substantially to healthcare outcomes if widely adopted. Designers of continuing education for clinicians should help provide opportunities for clinicians to improve their familiarity, use, and competency with AI tools, to help maximize the potential health benefits possible for patients and communities.

items.title: Assessing the Efficiency and Ergonomic Benefits of Artificial Intelligence–Assisted Acquisition
items.abstract: Objective: The aim of this study was to evaluate the effect of artificial intelligence (AI) assistance on examination efficiency and ergonomics during cardiac sonography. Materials and Methods: Randomized, cross-over study design was used with an ultrasound equipment system, cardiovascular software, and integrated AI features. A cohort of experienced sonographers (N = 30) performed standardized examinations with and without AI features enabled. All participating sonographers were new equipment users. Metrics of timing with and without AI assistance were acquired. Movements of the non-scanning hand were recorded during a subset of studies to assess time spent in a predefined ergonomic zone. Results: Artificial intelligence assistance reduced mean examination time by 10.16 ± 0.95 minutes (95% CI, 12.10-8.22; P < .001) independent of experience, age, scanning sequence, or prior AI familiarity. A sub-analysis of hand motion during sonography (n = 9) found AI assistance reduced average distance traveled by 50% (47.9 m) compared with unassisted examinations (SD, 10.6; 95% CI, 39.74-55.97, P < .01). Conclusion: In this cohort of users, AI-assisted cardiac sonography significantly reduced acquisition time and increased time spent within their optimal hand reach. This kind of upgrade may help lower the risk of work-related musculoskeletal injuries in cardiac sonographers. Further studies, based on actual clinical settings, would help to further clarify these benefits.

items.title: Autonomous Agentic AI Frameworks and Multi-Agent Collaboration: Architectures, Consensus Protocols, and Quantitative Benchmarks
items.abstract: Abstract—The transition from static, single-prompt Large Language Models (LLMs) toward autonomous agentic architectures represents a major paradigm shift in artificial intelligence and computer systems engineering. Modern autonomous agents perceive, reason, formulate multi-step plans, invoke dynamic tools via application programming interfaces (APIs), and iteratively correct operational trajectories. When orchestrated into Multi-Agent Systems (MAS), these discrete cognitive units achieve collaborative problem-solving capabilities far exceeding individual models. However, realizing reliable MAS deployments introduces severe challenges in multi-agent consensus protocols, cognitive memory hierarchies, cascading hallucination mitigation, token consumption economics, and execution safety. This paper presents an exhaustive technical survey and rigorous architectural synthesis of contemporary agentic AI frameworks—including LangGraph, AutoGen, CrewAI, and MetaGPT. We formalize agent cognitive workflows as Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) augmented by Tree-of-Thought (ToT) deliberation, analyze inter-agent communication topologies (hierarchical, peer-to-peer peer-review, and blackboard memory sharing), and formulate distributed consensus models under stochastic inference noise. Furthermore, we conduct a standardized empirical benchmark across four mission-critical domains (complex software synthesis, strategic decision-making, automated vulnerability discovery, and enterprise analytics). Our quantitative findings demonstrate that while hierarchical agent orchestrations achieve up to 34.8% higher task success rates over baseline chain-of-thought prompting, unconstrained peer-to-peer communications suffer exponential token overhead and vulnerability to deadlock. Finally, we formulate open research questions regarding mechanistic interpretability in agent negotiation, formal safety boundary verifications, and post-quantum cryptographic communication guarantees. Index Terms—Agentic AI, Autonomous Agents, Multi-Agent Systems (MAS), Foundation Models, Consensus Protocols, LangGraph, AutoGen, MetaGPT, Dynamic Replanning, Tool Augmented Generation.

items.abstract: The rapid evolution of Industry 4.0 and 5.0 demands flexible manufacturing systems that move beyond traditional rigid automation. This paper presents an integrated framework for Autonomous Mobile Manipulators (AMMs) driven by Edge Artificial Intelligence (AI) and advanced computer vision. By combining simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) with multi-axis force-torque sensing, the proposed system bridges the gap between autonomous mobility and precise robotic manipulation. Experimental evaluations in a simulated smart-factory environment demonstrate a 31% reduction in component transfer time, zero safety incidents during close human-cobot interactions, and a 96% first-attempt pick success rate for variable parts. This study highlights the viability of deploying collaborative mobile manipulators to achieve highly adaptable, human-centric production lines.

items.title: Balancing Efficiency and Human Oversight in AI-Driven ESG Audits: The Roles of AI Automation and Decision Making
items.abstract: The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) audits has created new opportunities to enhance corporate governance through faster and more consistent assurance processes. However, concerns remain regarding accountability, transparency, and the role of human oversight in AI-assisted auditing. Prior research has predominantly examined AI adoption in traditional financial auditing, leaving its role in the more qualitative and judgment-intensive context of ESG assurance comparatively underexplored, particularly with respect to how AI decision-making authority should be balanced against human oversight. This study examines the effects of AI automation and AI decision making on audit efficiency, accountability, and transparency, while assessing the mediating role of human oversight. A quantitative research design was adopted, and data were collected from 150 professionals involved in ESG audit-related functions (including ESG auditors, compliance officers, sustainability managers, and AI governance analysts) across private, public, and non-governmental organizations, recruited through purposive and snowball sampling via professional networks, audit forums, and LinkedIn ESG groups. The data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings indicate that AI automation significantly improves audit efficiency, accountability, and transparency. Similarly, AI decision making within governance structures exerts positive effects on all three outcome dimensions. Furthermore, human oversight partially mediates these relationships, strengthening the overall impact of AI on ESG audit outcomes. These results suggest that AI enhances ESG auditing effectiveness, but its benefits are maximized when supported by strong governance and human supervision. The study contributes to the emerging literature on AI-enabled ESG assurance by demonstrating the importance of balancing technological efficiency with accountability and transparency in corporate governance.

items.title: Behind the AI policies: A critical examination of the underlying conceptions of assessment in higher education
items.abstract: Abstract The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has prompted universities to develop policies regulating its use in teaching, learning, and assessment. Little empirical research has examined how they conceptualise assessment, and the assumptions underpinning their normative frameworks. This study addresses this gap through a comparative analysis of GenAI-related policy documents from 14 universities in Switzerland and Spain. Drawing on Chan's AI Ecological Education Policy Framework and Bacchi's problematisation theory, we use collaborative consensus-based coding to examine pedagogical, governance, and operational dimensions alongside problem representations, assumptions, subject positions, and silences. The findings reveal coexisting and sometimes competing representations of GenAI. Concerns about academic integrity, authorship, transparency, and data protection coexist with calls for AI literacy, assessment redesign, formative feedback, and critical engagement with AI. Assessment emerges as a key site of this tension, with policies combining AI-resistant approaches with attempts to integrate GenAI into educational processes. The analysis also reveals asymmetrical subject positions: teachers and institutions generally define legitimate AI use, whereas students are positioned as accountable users expected to disclose, justify, or verify their use of AI. AI literacy and evaluative judgement are likewise framed mainly as students competencies, leaving teachers corresponding needs less examined. Current GenAI policy therefore represent an important but incomplete response to AI-driven change. Future policy development should move beyond regulating acceptable use towards participatory and pedagogically grounded frameworks that involve students more actively in shaping AI-mediated assessment and support human agency, evaluative judgement, and meaningful learning.

items.title: Beyond financial literacy: The role of trust and neuropsychiatric symptoms in fraud vulnerability in dementia
items.abstract: ABSTRACT BACKGROUND Fraud vulnerability is an increasing concern in aging populations, particularly as financial activities shift to digital environments. Individuals with neurocognitive disorders may be especially vulnerable, yet the relative contribution of financial literacy, behavioral functioning, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and interpersonal factors remains poorly understood. This study examined these determinants in individuals with neurocognitive disorders. METHODS 290 individuals with neurocognitive disorders, including Alzheimer’s disease, frontotemporal dementia, Lewy body dementia, semantic dementia, and mild cognitive impairment, were enrolled. Financial vulnerability was assessed using the Financial Frailty Battery, a caregiver-administered instrument evaluating financial behaviors before and after disease onset. Neuropsychiatric symptoms were assessed with the Neuropsychiatric Inventory. Regression models examined predictors of fraud occurrence, fraud type, and fraud frequency. RESULTS Behavioral changes in everyday functioning and interpersonal trust emerged as the strongest correlates of fraud vulnerability. Behavioral tendencies (OR = 1.10, 95% CI [1.01, 1.19], p = .030) and trust (OR = 1.11, 95% CI [1.04, 1.18], p < .001) significantly predicted fraud victimization. Higher trust predicted non-digital (OR = 1.12, p = .005) and mixed fraud (OR = 1.19, p < .001), but not digital-only fraud (OR = 1.08, p = .101). Trust was also associated with repeated victimization (χ 2 (2) = 42.2, p < .001). CONCLUSIONS Fraud vulnerability in neurocognitive disorders appears to be driven primarily by behavioral and interpersonal factors rather than financial knowledge alone. Preliminary evidence suggests partially different vulnerability profiles for digital and non-digital fraud, highlighting the need for prevention strategies tailored to different forms of financial exploitation.

items.title: Beyond the Monolithic Interface: A Research Agenda for Plural Conversational AI
items.abstract: The current paradigm of artificial intelligence (AI) design elevates conversational chatbot interfaces, making them the default mode through which hundreds of millions of people interact with AI systems globally. This narrative review identifies three related harms produced by the single-voice chatbot interface, drawing on insights from literature in cognitive science, political studies, AI alignment, game design and human computer interaction. Firstly, cognitive offloading of user thinking, secondly, ideological narrowing of user beliefs, and thirdly, epistemic compression of cultural and value diversity. We then propose multi-persona interfaces, in which multiple personas are presented to the user simultaneously, as a cost-effective intervention that addresses all three harms at once. We ground this intervention in traditions the AI literature has largely overlooked, drawing on techniques from game design and participatory simulation, including the magic circle, role differentiation, and persona embodiment. We propose a taxonomy for the future design of multi-persona interfaces, and call for a research agenda that closes the gap between technical pluralistic alignment methods and empirical studies of human-AI interactions with pluralistic interfaces.

items.title: Bridging the AI use–competence gap
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming graduate research and academic work; however, increased use does not necessarily lead to critical evaluation or responsible engagement. This study examines the gap between graduate students’ AI use and their evaluative, ethical, and rhetorical engagement with AI-generated outputs. Using a survey-based exploratory case study design, the study draws on data from 50 graduate students across four national contexts, complemented by open-ended responses and contextual observations. Findings reveal high levels of AI use alongside limited verification practices, ethical uncertainty, and a tendency to view AI outputs as neutral or authoritative, indicating a persistent use–competence gap. items.title: Can machines reason non-verbally?
items.abstract: Modern machines can solve equations, follow logic and reason through language, yet they still struggle with problems that require visual non-verbal reasoning. This is evident even in advanced systems such as DeepSeek, ChatGPT and Gemini, which remain limited on visual tasks such as completing abstract patterns or delineating ambiguous regions-of-interest. Unlike explicit intermediate steps in verbal reasoning which can be verified through logic or automated tests, visual reasoning involves implicit intermediate steps with no clear methods for verification. Non-verbal reasoning is therefore challenging to model and, as a result, remains a fundamental limitation of current machine intelligence. Here we introduce GenVerOpt, a general framework that unifies generation, verification and optimisation into a reasoning pipeline for machines. By generating candidate solutions, verifying their correctness, and iteratively refining them, GenVerOpt enables per-sample optimisation rather than relying solely on dataset-level trends captured during model training. This process mirrors human problem-solving where multiple possibilities are imagined, evaluated, and refined until a correct solution emerges. Across diverse domains, GenVerOpt demonstrates capabilities beyond existing systems: it surpasses humans on abstract IQ puzzles, matches clinicians in prostate cancer segmentation, exceeds experts in liver vessel reconstruction and outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in tumour boundary alignment. These results show that machine reasoning can extend beyond language, establishing visual non-verbal reasoning as a foundation for more flexible and generalisable intelligence.

items.title: Cognitive Ergonomics in Robotics
items.abstract: Work tasks performed by humans within any work system are the connecting elements between humans and other system elements such as deployed technologies. Fundamental to any task performance are mental processes of those individuals acting within any socio-technical system. Perception, attention, learning, memory and reasoning are just examples of these processes. Within human factors, they are typically studied to evaluate, for instance, mental workload and situation awareness of technology users, whose errors can dramatically impact the safety and the performance of the system. Accordingly, this chapter presents concepts from cognitive ergonomics. These concepts should be considered within Human–Robot Interaction (HRI) studies and applications in order to assess and improve the design of robots which can interact with humans in terms of technology acceptance, usability, accessibility, and, overall, user experience. This chapter describes different effects on humans related to the interaction with robotic systems. Furthermore, specific HRI design elements and recommendations will be outlined. The chapter closes with an overview on quantitative and qualitative methods proposed to evaluate and to assess different aspects of HRI.

items.title: Community pharmacists’ acceptance and willingness to adopt artificial intelligence for medication counseling: a cross-sectional study in Jordan
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly being incorporated into healthcare delivery. This study aimed to assess pharmacists' perceptions, acceptance, and readiness to adopt Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies to support medication counseling in community pharmacy practice. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 300 community pharmacists in Jordan between February and March 2026. Acceptance of AI was assessed using the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). The survey collected data on perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, behavioral intention, prior AI experience, perceived benefits, and concerns regarding AI use. Logistic regression analysis was performed to identify factors associated with willingness to adopt AI in medication counseling. This study included a total of 300 community pharmacists. Overall, pharmacists demonstrated positive perceptions of AI technologies. Most participants were familiar with AI tools (n = 283, 94.3%) and reported using them in daily life (n = 222, 74.0%), although most had not received formal AI training (n = 185, 61.7%). More than half were willing to integrate AI into medication counseling (n = 156, 52.0%), while 104 (34.7%) were uncertain and 40 (13.3%) were unwilling. The most commonly perceived benefits were improved patient education (n = 204, 68.0%), drug interaction checking (n = 200, 66.7%), and counseling efficiency (n = 197, 65.7%). Major concerns included inadequate regulation (n = 218, 72.7%), AI accuracy (n = 205, 68.3%), and data privacy (n = 205, 68.3%). Our model demonstrates that behavioral intent is the primary source of willingness to adopt AI (AOR = 1.966, 95% CI: 1.212–3.188; p = 0.006), while younger age was also associated with greater willingness (AOR = 0.947, 95% CI: 0.915–0.980; p = 0.002). Community pharmacists generally viewed AI as a valuable adjunct to medication counseling rather than a replacement for professional judgment. Addressing concerns related to regulation, training, data privacy, and AI reliability will be essential for the successful integration of AI into pharmacy practice.

items.title: Creativity in design education: an educational psychology model of motivation, cognitive load, and self-efficacy
items.abstract: Objective This study examines the statistical relationships among learning motivation, cognitive load, creative self-efficacy, and expert-rated creative performance among undergraduate design students. Methods A quantitative cross-sectional study was conducted with 428 valid responses from undergraduate students majoring in design-related disciplines. Students first completed a design task, after which questionnaire data were collected and anonymized design works were evaluated by three independent experts. SPSS was used for descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, correlation analysis, regression-based path analysis, and Bootstrap tests of statistical indirect effects; AMOS was used to evaluate the measurement model. Results Learning motivation and germane cognitive load were positively associated with creative self-efficacy. Creative self-efficacy showed the strongest positive association with design creative performance, and germane cognitive load showed a smaller positive direct association. Extraneous cognitive load was negatively correlated with creative performance at the bivariate level, but its adjusted direct path was not statistically significant; therefore, H5 was not supported. Intrinsic cognitive load was not significant. Bootstrap results indicated significant statistical indirect relationships through creative self-efficacy. Conclusion The findings suggest that design creativity is associated with students' motivation, meaningful cognitive engagement, and creative self-beliefs. Because the questionnaire was administered after the design task, the indirect effects should be interpreted as statistical indirect relationships rather than evidence of causal or temporal mediation.

items.title: Devising a Principled Rapid Guessing Workflow: Identification, Impact, and Treatment of Rapid Guessing in Cognitive Assessment
items.abstract: Abstract Low‐stakes assessments are particularly vulnerable to rapid guessing behavior, where responses may reflect minimal cognitive engagement, potentially biasing scores and weakening inferences. Drawing on a scoping review of more than 70 studies, we summarize how rapid guessing is identified, its impact on key parameters, and how it is treated. Detection methods range from time‐based thresholds to statistical models using response‐time or residual data, each balancing practicality and precision. Treatments include filtering, downweighting, and model‐based adjustments, with differing consequences for score meaning and comparability. However, decisions about identifying rapid guessing, evaluating its impact, and selecting treatments are often not explicitly linked, making it difficult to arrive at coherent analytic choices. To address this, we propose a four‐step workflow and reporting guidelines: (1) clarify construct relevance, (2) screen using context‐appropriate methods, (3) assess impact via sensitivity analysis, and (4) justify a treatment. Together, these tools provide a practical framework for defensible educational measurement practice.

items.abstract: As undergraduate research increasingly relies on digital databases, analytical software, and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled technologies, research learning is potentially mediated through digital infrastructures that enable students to engage in knowledge construction. However, disparities in technological access and institutional support may constrain these learning opportunities. Guided by van Dijk’s digital divide model and Ragnedda’s concept of digital capital, this study employed interpretative phenomenological analysis (IPA) to examine how undergraduate students experienced digital readiness during the research process. Data were generated through three rounds of in-depth interviews with each of the eight undergraduate researchers at a Vietnamese public university. Analysis revealed that limited access to scholarly databases and research software usually restricted students’ engagement with technology-enhanced research learning. In addition, the absence of clear institutional policies and guidance regarding AI technologies potentially generated uncertainty about acceptable AI practices and contributed to uneven development of students’ digital competencies. These technological constraints influenced many students’ academic self-efficacy and reduced their ability to transform digital resources into meaningful learning and research outcomes. The effectiveness of technology-supported undergraduate research might depend not only on the availability of digital tools but also on equitable access, AI literacy development, and institutional support structures. The study contributes to the field of technologies in learning by demonstrating how digital infrastructure and technology governance may shape students’ participation in research-based learning. Implications are offered for the design of inclusive technology-enabled learning environments that support equitable undergraduate research engagement.

items.title: DIGITAL STORYTELLING AND NARRATIVE IN THE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AGE: TRANSFORMING CREATIVITY, COMMUNICATION, AND HUMAN EXPERIENCE
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed the landscape of digital storytelling, reshaping how narratives are created, shared, and experienced across various digital platforms. From automated content generation and interactive storytelling to virtual reality experiences and personalized narratives, AI has become an influential creative partner in media production, education, entertainment, journalism, marketing, and cultural preservation. This paper examines the evolving relationship between digital storytelling and artificial intelligence, focusing on how AI influences creativity, communication, and human experience. Using a qualitative review of existing literature, the study explores the historical evolution of storytelling, the emergence of AI-powered narrative systems, and the opportunities and challenges associated with AI-assisted creativity. The paper also discusses ethical concerns, including algorithmic bias, misinformation, copyright ownership, authenticity, and the changing role of human creators. Findings suggest that while AI enhances efficiency, personalization, and audience engagement, human imagination, emotional intelligence, cultural awareness, and ethical judgment remain indispensable components of meaningful storytelling. The study concludes that the future of storytelling lies in collaborative intelligence, where humans and AI work together to produce innovative, inclusive, and emotionally resonant narratives.

items.title: Digital technologies and operational efficiency: evidence from small and medium enterprises in Lagos State, Nigeria
items.abstract: Digital technologies enable businesses to secure and manage information, which can be accessed at any time, allowing authorised users to make decisions more efficiently. Despite this potential, many SMEs in Nigeria are unable to fully maximise digital technologies, which limits their operational efficiency and competitiveness. This paper examined the impact of digital technologies on operational efficiency of SMEs in Lagos State, Nigeria, using a quantitative survey research design. A structured questionnaire was used to collect data from 166 SME owners, and both stratified and purposive sampling techniques were employed. Data were analysed using descriptive and inferential-regression analyses, while the paper was anchored on the technology acceptance and diffusion of innovation theories. The findings indicate that artificial intelligence and cloud computing play significant roles in product forecasting and improving business processes, but do not significantly contribute to inventory management. The paper further reveals that the effects of digital technologies are situational, requiring appropriate system integration, personnel capacity building, and alignment of operational processes. These findings can guide Lagos State SME managers and policymakers in enhancing efficiency, competitiveness, and sustainable business development.

items.title: DIGITALIZATION AS A DRIVER OF ECONOMIC GROWTH AND STRUCTURAL TRANSFORMATION
items.abstract: Digitalization has become an important factor influencing economic growth, productivity, employment, innovation and the structural transformation of economies. The expansion of broadband networks, cloud computing, digital platforms, artificial intelligence, big data analytics, digital financial services and other information and communication technologies has changed the organization of production and the allocation of economic resources. This article examines the mechanisms through which digitalization contributes to economic growth and structural transformation, with particular attention to productivity, innovation, sectoral reallocation, labor markets, trade and the development of digital services. The study is based on a review and comparative analysis of evidence from the World Bank, OECD, International Telecommunication Union, UN Trade and Development and peer-reviewed academic literature. The evidence indicates that digital technologies can increase productivity by reducing transaction costs, improving information flows, facilitating automation, supporting innovation and expanding access to markets. However, the economic effects of digitalization are not automatic. Productivity gains depend on complementary investments in human capital, organizational capabilities, physical and digital infrastructure, competition and institutional quality. Digitalization can also contribute to structural transformation by facilitating the movement of economic activity toward higher-productivity manufacturing and service activities and by creating new digitally enabled occupations and business models. At the same time, differences in connectivity, affordability, digital skills and access to capital can cause the benefits of digital transformation to be distributed unevenly. The article concludes that digitalization should be treated not simply as technological modernization but as a broad economic transformation requiring coordinated policies in infrastructure, skills, innovation, competition and data governance.

items.title: Dispositional foundations for AI-mediated learning: evidence from a latent profile analysis of grade-8 students in ICILS 2023
items.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) becomes increasingly integrated into education, understanding whether students possess the foundational conditions needed to benefit from AI-mediated learning has become an important educational challenge. This study conceptualizes dispositional foundations for AI-mediated learning as the configuration of ICT self-efficacy, attitudes toward technology and expectations of future ICT use that may support meaningful engagement with AI-mediated learning environments, and examines how these configurations relate to objectively assessed digital competence and to student characteristics. ICILS 2023 contains no measure of AI literacy or AI use, so these are candidate foundations rather than a direct measure of preparedness for AI. Using data from 118,764 Grade-8 students across 35 education systems participating in the International Computer and Information Literacy Study (ICILS 2023), we conducted sampling-weighted latent profile analyses on four internationally comparable indicators. Computer and information literacy (CIL) was examined as an external criterion using the BCH approach, and profile membership was predicted by socioeconomic background, gender, educational aspirations and ICT access. Four profiles emerged: average (55.9%), attitude-oriented (25.2%), low-disposition (11.0%) and efficacy-dominant (7.9%). Differences in CIL across profiles were modest, and students in the efficacy-dominant profile, who reported ICT self-efficacy more than two standard deviations above the mean, did not outperform the average profile in objectively assessed competence, a pattern we interpret as a confidence-competence mismatch rather than as high preparedness. On a common metric of average marginal effects, gender showed larger and more consistent contrasts than socioeconomic background. These findings suggest that the dispositional foundations for AI-mediated learning are distinct from computer and information literacy and should be understood as a multidimensional configuration of learner characteristics whose relevance to actual AI-mediated learning remains to be tested directly.

items.title: Do-It-with-AI Framework for Invention: A Kundt’s Tube Case Study
items.abstract: This exploratory case study examines the feasibility of integrating generative artificial intelligence (AI) into a low-cost Kundt’s tube activity in pre-service science teacher education. The proposed Do-It-With-AI framework comprises four phases: conceptual exploration, design development, troubleshooting, and extension to real-world applications. Scopus AI was used to support the literature-oriented conceptual exploration, while ChatGPT-4 and ChatGPT-5 supported the generation of design alternatives, troubleshooting hypotheses, and possible extensions. Three pre-service teachers constructed and tested the apparatus, and successive configurations were evaluated through resonance measurements and estimation of the speed of sound. The case illustrates how AI-generated suggestions can be incorporated into an iterative design–test–verification process in which proposed modifications are examined against physical principles and experimental evidence. The four-phase sequence is therefore presented as a feasible framework for integrating generative AI with hands-on experimentation, with instructor-guided verification serving as an essential component. Because the present study focuses on feasibility and process rather than educational outcomes, further investigation with larger cohorts and explicit measures of student reasoning, learning, collaboration, and AI literacy is required. The principal contribution of the Kundt’s tube case is to demonstrate a structured and empirically grounded use of generative AI in low-cost experimental development within pre-service science teacher education.

items.title: Ecological Invisibility in Classroom AI Use: Rethinking Pedagogical Efficiency, Sustainability and Teacher Agency
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in everyday teaching, yet its environmental costs remain largely absent from how educators reason about its use. This study examines how 22 teachers working in public schools in Türkiye, each with at least one academic year of experience integrating artificial intelligence into the classroom, interpret and navigate these technologies at the intersection of pedagogical effectiveness, professional responsibility, and ecological sustainability. Semi-structured interviews were analyzed through Braun and Clarke’s reflexive thematic analysis within a generic interpretive qualitative design. Five themes were developed. The first three show teachers actively mediating AI through pedagogical judgment, a restructured professional agency, and a renewed relational and epistemic role. The study’s central contribution lies in the final two: for almost all participants, AI’s ecological cost was not unknown but rendered invisible in everyday practice—a professionally produced ordering of attention enacted through the very pedagogical agency that makes teachers effective. When this cost surfaced, teachers managed rather than resolved the tension through pedagogical rationalization and self-reported intentions toward ecologically motivated restraint, while extending their moral concern to students’ cognitive dependence. Ecological invisibility thus emerges not as a knowledge deficit but as a by-product of professional attention—one that teacher education and policy should address through a critical AI literacy integrating ethical, ecological, and pedagogical dimensions.

items.title: Emotional Comfort at a Cost: The Dynamic Role of Social Chatbot Use in Daily Loneliness, Well-Being, and Interpersonal Interaction
items.abstract: As generative AI chatbots increasingly serve as emotional companions, understanding their implications for users’ emotional and social lives is critical. This 14-day diary study involving 97 social chatbot users examined how daily loneliness relates to chatbot engagement and subsequent psychosocial outcomes. Bayesian multilevel models showed that on days when participants felt lonelier than usual, they reported longer chatbot use and stronger emotional engagement. Notably, these two forms of engagement showed distinct associations with daily outcomes. Emotional engagement was associated with higher daily subjective well-being but shorter interpersonal interaction duration, whereas longer usage duration was associated with lower interpersonal interaction pleasure. Mediation analyses reflected the same patterns. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing behavioral from emotional engagement with social chatbots and suggest that emotional benefits and interpersonal costs may coexist in everyday human–AI interaction, informing the responsible design and balanced use of social AI companions.

items.title: Employee AI readiness and the leadership gap: a theory-informed commentary on a CIO.com feature
items.abstract: This paper offers a theory-informed commentary on the executive-employee gap in enterprise artificial intelligence (AI) readiness, using a CIO.com feature on employee AI optimism and an AI leadership gap as its focal practitioner text. Rather than treating the article as empirical evidence, the paper interprets it through scholarship on socio-technical change, organizational readiness, AI governance, work design, and incentive alignment, using 2024-2025 industry reports as context. It examines how the text frames the readiness gap, how socio-technical and incentive-alignment perspectives explain it, and what operational risks may follow. The analysis suggests the leadership gap is better understood as an organizational-design problem than as employee resistance or a training deficit. When AI tools are introduced without changes to workflows, governance, learning, and accountability, employees may face burdens and uncertainty about legitimate AI use. The paper contributes by framing AI readiness as an organizational condition, integrating socio-technical and incentive-alignment perspectives, identifying shadow AI, weak output validation, data-quality problems, and accountability ambiguity as risk pathways, and proposing a Socio-Technical AI Readiness Framework linking AI pressure, readiness architecture, employee readiness, operational transformation, and risk leakage. For managers, sustainable AI transformation requires credible organizational conditions for AI-enabled work, not merely greater tool use.
